slides.title: One button, six and a half seconds of waiting
slides.tldr: Send the email, SMS, PDF and courier call inside the order request and the customer waits, and one failure breaks everything.

blocks.title: The pizza place's cashier
blocks.body: Picture a cashier at a pizza place who takes your order, walks into the kitchen to make the pizza, boxes it and goes hunting for a delivery driver, and only then calls the next customer. The queue spills onto the street, and if the delivery driver can't be found, the whole order is canceled. A smarter cashier takes the money, writes a slip, sends it to the kitchen and calls the next person. The controller below is the first cashier.

marks.tip: This one line is all the customer needs: the order is now in the database.
If the mail server is slow, the whole request is slow, yet nobody would mind the email arriving ten seconds later.
If the courier API is down, an exception is thrown here. The customer sees "order failed" even though the order is saved.

blocks.caption: Where the 6.4 seconds of one request went

items.label: Save order
items.tip: The only step you can't skip: without it there is no order number to give the customer.

items.label: Email
items.tip: Waiting for an external mail server to answer. It can safely go out later.

items.label: SMS
items.tip: Waiting for the SMS gateway. When the gateway is slow, this can stretch to 30 seconds.

items.label: Invoice PDF
items.tip: Heavy CPU work, and the customer isn't opening the PDF right now anyway.

items.label: Courier API
items.tip: The slowest and most fragile step: another company's server, which you don't control.

blocks.code:
#[Route('/orders', methods: ['POST'])]
public function create(#[MapRequestPayload] CreateOrder $dto): JsonResponse
{
    $order = $this->orders->place($dto, $this->getUser());    // 40ms

    $this->bus->dispatch(new OrderPlaced($order->getId()));   // about 2ms: a note in the queue

    return $this->json(['id' => $order->getId()], 201);       // about 42ms in total
}

marks.tip: One note replaces four slow calls. The email, SMS, PDF and courier jobs become handlers that a worker runs later, so a slow courier API can no longer break the order.

blocks.body: Make the user wait only for what the response truly needs.

aside.title: Triple orders on sale night
aside.body: On sale night an online shop's SMS gateway slowed down. The SMS was sent inside the order request, so every order took half a minute. Impatient customers kept hitting "Place order", and the same order was created three times. The problem was in the SMS, but the orders broke.

items.meaning: Standing there and waiting until the work is finished.
Writing "to be done later" on a note and getting back to your own work.

items.label: Keeping one failure from spreading to others

check.q: Which of the controller's five jobs must stay inside the request, and why?
check.a: Only saving the order, because without it there is no order number to give the customer. The email, SMS, PDF and courier booking can happen a few seconds later without hurting anyone.

slides.title: A command says "do this", an event says "this happened"
slides.tldr: A command orders one specific handler to do a job. An event only announces what happened, and zero or many listeners react on their own.

blocks.title: The kitchen slip and the counter bell
blocks.body: The cashier sends a slip to the kitchen: "Table 5, two large pepperoni pizzas." That's a **command**: an order for one specific person, and the job has to get done. The cashier can also ring a bell and announce, "Order 42 is in." That's an **event**: the cook, the accountant and the delivery driver each hear it and pick up their own work, and the cashier never knows who is listening.

blocks.caption: The same order, two kinds of message

columns.title: Command
items: Named as an order: SendInvoiceEmail
Exactly one handler
The sender knows who does the job
A new job means changing the sender's code
columns.tip: An order to do a job. The sender knows who it is talking to and expects the job to be done.

columns.title: Event
items: Named in the past tense: OrderPlaced
Zero, one or many handlers
The sender doesn't know who is listening
A new job is just a new handler
columns.tip: An announcement of something that already happened. The sender has no need to know who listens.

blocks.body: The real difference isn't the name but **who knows whom**. Send commands, and the order code knows about the email, the courier and the invoice. Publish an event, and the order code knows nobody. If you add "loyalty points" tomorrow, you don't touch the order code at all. The price: nobody can read in one place what an order sets off, so list the listeners with `debug:messenger`.

marks.tip: Every new job is a change to the sender, and a bug here can break ordering itself.
The sender never changes. Each listener is its own handler class that subscribes to `OrderPlaced`.

blocks.body: A command says "do this". An event says "this happened".

items: Start command names with a verb: `GenerateInvoicePdf`, `BookCourier`.
Put event names in the past tense: `OrderPlaced`, `PaymentFailed`.
An event carries what happened and an id, not instructions about who should do what.

use: An event, when several independent things react to a fact, or more reactions are likely to be added later.
A command, when one specific job must happen and the sender cares that it does.
avoid: An event for a step the flow cannot continue without. Hidden listeners make a required step easy to lose.

items: An event called `OrderPlacedSendEmail` is a command in disguise: the sender is again telling the listener what to do.
If the sender waits for a listener's result, it is no longer an event. Use a direct method call or a command.

check.q: After an order you need an email, a courier booking and loyalty points. Which approach means fewer changes to the order code later, and why?
check.a: An event (`OrderPlaced`). The order code only announces the fact, and three separate handlers listen. When a fourth job shows up, you add a handler and never touch the order code.

slides.title: Symfony Messenger: message, handler, transport, worker
slides.tldr: A message is a small DTO, the handler does the job, the transport stores the message, and a worker in a separate process picks it up and runs the handler.

blocks.body: Messenger has four parts. The controller just calls `$bus->dispatch(new OrderPlaced($order->getId()))` and returns immediately. The message is stored in a **transport** (a queue), and a separate process, the **worker**, picks it up and runs the **handler**. Remember: without a `routing` entry, the handler runs inside the request itself and nothing is async.

blocks.caption: The journey of one OrderPlaced message

nodes.label: Controller
nodes.tip: After saving the order it only hands the message to the bus. There is no email-sending code here.

nodes.label: Message bus
nodes.tip: Looks at the message class and decides: run the handler now, or send the message to a transport.

nodes.label: Transport: async
nodes.tip: Where messages wait: a Doctrine table, RabbitMQ, SQS or Redis. The message stays safe here until a worker picks it up.

nodes.label: Worker
nodes.tip: A separate, long-running PHP process. It has nothing to do with web requests.

nodes.label: Handler
nodes.tip: The code that does the real work. If it is slow or fails here, the customer never notices.

nodes.label: Customer
nodes.tip: Has the order number after 40 milliseconds. The email arrives a few seconds later.

edges.label: The controller hands the message to the bus
Routing says this message goes to the async transport
The customer gets a response right away, with work still pending
A worker takes the message off the queue
It matches the message class and runs the right handler

marks.tip: Only the id goes in the message. A whole entity would reach the worker as a stale copy, because the order can change while the message waits in the queue.
This attribute tells Messenger that the class type-hinted in `__invoke()` is the message this handler handles.
The handler reads a fresh copy of the order from the database every time.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        transports:
            # doctrine://default, amqp://… or sqs://… — the code doesn't change
            async: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'

        routing:
            # without this line the handler runs inside the request
            'App\Message\OrderPlaced': async

marks.tip: To switch transports, change only the DSN in `.env`. A small app can start with the Doctrine transport and needs no extra server, but it polls your database, so move to RabbitMQ or SQS as volume grows.
Message class → transport. If the class isn't listed here, Messenger sends the message nowhere and runs the handler on the spot.

items.desc: Start a worker; -vv prints every message as it is handled
List which handler handles which message
Show how many messages are waiting in each transport
Stop workers after a deploy so they restart with the new code

items: Workers run for a long time, so after a deploy the old code stays in memory. Run `messenger:stop-workers` on every deploy.
In production run workers under Supervisor or systemd so they come back up on their own after stopping.
Use `--time-limit=3600` or `--memory-limit=128M` so workers restart themselves regularly.

items.label: When a handler fails: retries and the DLQ

check.q: What exactly happens if you forget to list the message class under routing in messenger.yaml?
check.a: Messenger sends the message to no transport, and the handler runs inside `dispatch()`, so inside the request. The code works, but nothing is async.

slides.title: Queue vs stream: the order spike and the ledger
slides.tldr: A queue gives each message to one worker and deletes it when done. A stream keeps every message in order, and each reader reads from its own position.

blocks.title: The order spike and the ledger
blocks.body: The ticket spike on the kitchen counter, where order slips are pushed onto a metal spindle, is a **queue**: one cook takes a slip, finishes the dish and tears the slip up, so nobody else ever sees it. The restaurant's ledger is a **stream**: every order is written in sequence and nobody erases it. The owner, the accountant and the tax auditor all read the whole ledger, each from their own bookmark, and any of them can start again from page one.

blocks.caption: Queue vs stream: who does what

rows.tip: Symfony Messenger's Doctrine, AMQP, SQS and Redis transports all behave like queues.
In a queue, an ack is the end of the message. In a stream, messages go away only when the retention period (say 7 days) runs out.
In a queue, workers share the same job. In a stream, each consumer group reads the entire ledger on its own.
An offset is a bookmark showing how far into the ledger a group has read. Each consumer group has its own.

cells: Move the offset back to replay
rows.tip: A new service added to a stream can read the whole history from the start. In a queue the old messages are already gone.

cells: An event history shared by many services
rows.tip: A queue splits up jobs and retries each message separately. A stream keeps an ordered history of events, useful for analytics, CDC and event sourcing.

blocks.title: Which to pick
items: "Do it once" jobs such as emails, PDFs and API calls → queue. For most apps that is enough.
Many services read the same events separately, or you need to replay old events → stream.
Running Kafka is a skill of its own. Stick with a queue until you can prove you need more.

items.meaning: The server that stores and delivers messages, such as RabbitMQ or Kafka.
A team of readers sharing one job; together they receive each message once.
The sequence number showing how far a reader has read in a stream.
How long a stream keeps its messages.

items: Installing Kafka just to send emails is using a cannon to swat a mosquito.
Treating a queue as a permanent history of events. Once a job is done the message is gone; keep history in the database or in a stream.

check.q: A new analytics service wants to read all order events from the last 7 days. Why is that impossible with a queue and possible with a stream?
check.a: In a queue, a message is deleted once a worker finishes it. In a stream, messages stay until the retention period ends, so a new consumer group can start reading from the very first offset.

slides.title: The trap: in the queue does not mean done
slides.tldr: dispatch() means the job was written down, not done. Make async an answer the user needs right now and you have to lie to them.

blocks.body: Async has a price: you don't know **when** the job will finish, the user may have left the page by the time it fails, and the same message can arrive twice. So if the user needs a result right now, you can't toss the job into a queue and say "done". The first code below says "paid" before any money has been taken.

blocks.code:
#[Route('/orders/{id}/pay', methods: ['POST'])]
#[IsGranted('PAY', subject: 'order')]
public function pay(Order $order, MessageBusInterface $bus): JsonResponse
{
    $bus->dispatch(new ChargeOrder($order->getId()));   // only written to the queue

    return $this->json(['status' => 'paid']);           // a lie: nothing charged yet
}

marks.tip: The worker may run 3 seconds from now, or fail. By then the customer has seen "payment successful" and closed the page.
Write the true state to the database and commit first, then dispatch. Do it the other way around and the worker looks for an order that isn't saved yet.
`202 Accepted` means "request received, not finished yet". The client uses `statusUrl` or live updates to learn the final result.
The state does not stay "pending" forever: the handler settles it to paid or failed, and the status URL shows whichever it became.

blocks.caption: Which work goes to the queue and which stays in the request

columns.title: Send to async
items: Slow work: email, SMS, PDF, reports
External APIs that can go down any time
Results you can learn a few seconds later
Jobs that can safely retry on their own after a failure
columns.tip: These jobs can finish a little later without hurting the user, and separating them keeps one failure away from the order.

columns.title: Keep in the request
items: Input validation
Checking and reserving stock or seats
Results the user needs to decide what to do next
Quick work that must sit in the same transaction
columns.tip: You can't tell the user the truth without these answers, so a short wait is the right call.

blocks.body: dispatch() means the job was written down, not done.

aside.body: Need to know now? Stay sync. Fine to know later? Go async, and answer with the true state: "pending".

items: Dispatch before the transaction commits and the worker may look for a row it can't see yet. Commit first, then dispatch.
Once work is async, the handler must be ready to run twice: the same message can arrive again.
Commit then dispatch can still lose the message if the app dies in between, leaving the order "pending" forever. The outbox pattern closes that gap.

items.label: Making commit and dispatch happen together: the outbox
Telling the user when the job finishes

check.q: After queuing the job, which status code and state is the honest answer from the API, and why?
check.a: `202 Accepted` with a `pending` state and a URL to check progress. Saying `200`/`paid` would be a lie: the job hasn't run yet and may still fail.

slides.title: Two confirmation emails for one order
slides.tldr: If a worker finishes the job but dies before sending the ack, the broker delivers the message again and the job runs twice.

blocks.title: The courier's signed receipt
blocks.body: A delivery driver drops off a package and gets the receipt signed, and only then does the office write "delivered". With no signature, the office assumes the package never arrived and sends another driver. Now suppose the package did arrive, but the driver's van broke down before he could collect the signature. The customer ends up with two packages.

blocks.caption: The email went out, the ack didn't, so the message came again

actors.label: Broker
actors.tip: Stores messages. It does not delete a message until it receives an ack.

actors.label: Worker
actors.tip: Takes the message and runs the handler. When the job is done, it is supposed to send an ack to the broker.

actors.label: Customer
actors.tip: The person whose inbox the email lands in.

messages.label: Take OrderPlaced #501
messages.tip: The message is delivered for the first time.

messages.label: Confirmation email goes out
messages.tip: The job really did get done.

messages.label: No ack, take #501 again
messages.tip: The broker can't know whether the job was done. Sending it again is the safe choice.

blocks.body: No ack means the broker can't tell whether the job was done, so it sends the message again.

aside.title: The double mobile top-up
aside.body: One app's "top up" handler sent money to the operator and then sent the ack. During a deploy a worker was shut down halfway through. A new worker received the same message again and topped up a second time.

items.meaning: The worker's signal saying "job done, you can delete the message".
The broker handing out the same message again because no ack arrived.

check.q: A worker sends the email and then dies before the ack. Why does the broker deliver the message again?
check.a: The broker can't tell whether the job was done. No ack means "maybe not", and redelivering is safer than losing the message.

slides.title: At-most-once, at-least-once and "exactly-once"
slides.tldr: Ack before the work and a message can be lost; ack after and it can arrive twice. Exactly-once is really at-least-once plus an idempotent handler.

blocks.title: When does the receipt get signed?
blocks.body: If the driver tells the office "delivered" the moment he picks up the package, nobody goes looking when it gets lost on the way. That's **at-most-once**. If he reports only after the customer has signed, a lost signature can send the package out twice. That's **at-least-once**. And if, on the second trip, the customer says "I already have this one, take it back", the result is exactly one package. That's **effectively-once**.

blocks.caption: The three guarantees side by side

rows.tip: The only difference is where the ack sits. Effectively-once acks exactly like at-least-once.
The first loses work and the second duplicates it. In the third, a duplicate can arrive and do no harm.
Live location or a metric sample can be lost because the next one is coming. For money, neither a loss nor a duplicate is acceptable.
The broker guarantees delivery, but handling the effect of duplicates is the handler's job.

blocks.body: There is no exactly-once delivery. There is at-least-once plus an idempotent handler.

aside.body: Networks and processes can die at any moment. So neither broker nor worker can be sure a job was done, and a delivery guarantee is the rule for handling that uncertainty.
Twice beats lost, and turning twice into once is the handler's job.

check.q: Kafka or SQS advertises "exactly-once". What should you still do in your handler?
check.a: Make it idempotent anyway. That guarantee usually holds only inside the broker, and outside work like your email or payment API can still run twice.

slides.title: Ordering and partitions: same key, same line
slides.tldr: With many workers running at once, message order breaks. Send messages with the same key to the same partition and the order holds within that key.

blocks.title: The bank counters
blocks.body: With four counters in a bank the queue moves fast, but if Ryan's deposit and withdrawal go to two different counters, nobody can say which finishes first. So the rule is that all of Ryan's work always goes to the same counter. His own transactions stay in order, while the counters together still work in parallel.

blocks.caption: The account id picks the partition, with one worker per partition

nodes.label: Producer
nodes.tip: Sends a key with every message, here the account id.

nodes.label: Partition 0
nodes.tip: Messages whose key hashes here stay in the order they came in.

nodes.label: Partition 1
nodes.tip: The line for the other keys. It runs in parallel with p0.

nodes.label: Worker A
nodes.tip: Only one reader at a time per partition, so the order can't break.

nodes.label: Worker B
nodes.tip: A separate worker, so throughput goes up.

edges.label: Messages for acc 7 are hashed to partition 0
Messages for acc 8 are hashed to partition 1
Worker A gets acc 7's messages in arrival order
Worker B runs its own line at the same time

blocks.title: What it is called where
items: Kafka: the message key picks the partition, and each partition has one reader per consumer group.
Amazon SQS FIFO: messages with the same `MessageGroupId` keep their order.
RabbitMQ: one consumer on a queue keeps order; with several consumers it doesn't.
Ask for a single global order across the whole system and every message lands in one line, so throughput stalls.
When one key runs too hot (a hot key), the single worker on that partition buckles under the load.

items.meaning: The value that decides which line a message goes to.
A key that has far more messages than the others.

check.q: You want the "deposit" and "withdrawal" messages of one account processed in order. What should the partition key be?
check.a: accountId. All messages of one account then reach one worker, in order, on one partition, while different accounts run in parallel.

slides.title: Handling ack, duplicates and order in Messenger
slides.tldr: Messenger acks only after the handler succeeds, so delivery is at-least-once. Skip repeats by message id, and set a group id only where order matters.

blocks.body: Messenger acks **after** the handler finishes, and doesn't ack when an exception is thrown. So the default is at-least-once, and the same `AccountCredited` message can reach the handler twice. The handler therefore writes each message's id into an `applied_events` table in the same transaction as the balance change. A repeat finds its id already there and does nothing. Order is a separate matter: set a message group only where it matters.

marks.tip: The group id is SQS's version of a partition key. Messages in one group run one after another.
SQS FIFO drops a second send with this id for 5 minutes. It does not stop a redelivery to the consumer, so the handler still needs its own check.
Id row and balance change commit together or not at all. Split them and a crash in between loses the credit or repeats it.
`id` is the primary key. 0 rows inserted means the id was already there. `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` is PostgreSQL and SQLite; MySQL uses `INSERT IGNORE`.
A skipped repeat returns normally, so Messenger acks it. It is not a failure.

blocks.title: The rules behind this code
items: The ack comes after the handler succeeds, so work is never lost, only repeated.
A change like "+50" is made safe by storing its id in the same transaction as its effect.
Use a group id only where order changes the result, such as "withdraw only if the balance covers it".
The price is one extra insert per message, and old ids must be deleted after a few days.
First ask whether you need order at all. Credits that only add up give the same total in any order, and emails or PDFs need none.
Delete `applied_events` rows older than the longest a message can still be redelivered, or the table grows forever.

check.q: What goes wrong if you give every message the same group id to guarantee order?
check.a: All messages end up in one line with one worker, so parallelism drops to zero. The group id should be a small unit such as one account or one order.

slides.title: "Apply only if newer" is for snapshots, not changes
slides.tldr: A version check drops late messages. That is right when a message carries the whole new state, and silently loses money when it carries only a change.

blocks.body: A tempting rule is "ignore any message whose version is older than the last one I applied". Try it on an account holding $100. Credit +50 (version 1) and credit +30 (version 2) are sent, but version 2 arrives first. The handler applies it (130), then drops version 1 as stale. The balance stays 130 instead of 180, and no error appears anywhere.

blocks.caption: Same two credits, arriving out of order, with three handlers

columns.title: Change + version check
items: Version 2 (+30) arrives first: 130
Version 1 (+50) arrives late: dropped as stale
Balance ends at 130, not 180
$50 vanish and nothing fails
columns.tip: The handler treats a late change as stale and throws it away. The change was real, so its money is gone.

columns.title: Change + stored ids
items: Version 2 (+30) arrives first: new id, 130
Version 1 (+50) arrives late: new id, 180
A redelivered +30: id already stored, skipped
Balance ends at 180, correct
columns.tip: Each change is applied once, whatever the order. Adding is order-independent, so the total comes out right.

columns.title: Snapshot + version check
items: Version 2 says "balance is 180": applied
Version 1 says "balance is 150": late, dropped
Balance ends at 180, correct
columns.tip: The newest snapshot already contains everything older ones said, so dropping a late one loses nothing.

blocks.file: bad: a change guarded by a version
blocks.code:
-- message = "+50, version 1"; the row is already at version 2
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + :amount, version = :version
WHERE id = :id AND version < :version;   -- 0 rows: the +50 is lost

marks.tip: For a change message this WHERE clause turns "arrived late" into "never happened".

blocks.file: good: a snapshot guarded by a version
blocks.code:
-- message = "balance is 150, version 1"; the row is already at version 2
UPDATE account_summaries
SET balance = :balance, version = :version
WHERE id = :id AND version < :version;   -- 0 rows: version 2 already says more

blocks.body: Drop a message as stale only if a newer message already contains it.

use: A version check, for messages that carry the whole new state, like "address is now X" or "balance is now 180".
Stored message ids, for changes like "+50", "stock -3" or "1 point earned".
avoid: A version check on a change message. It loses data and no error shows.

items.meaning: A message that says what the state is now.
A message that says only what changed, such as "+50".

check.q: From a balance of 100, "+50" (version 1) arrives after "+30" (version 2). A handler that drops older versions ends at what balance, and why?
check.a: 130. It drops version 1 as stale, so the +50 is lost. A change must be deduplicated by its id, never dropped for being old.

slides.title: The message that never succeeds
slides.tldr: Rerun a broken message again and again in a rush and a failing API takes even more pressure while the queue clogs up. You need a rule for cutting it off.

blocks.title: The letter with the wrong address
blocks.body: A postman can't find the house for one letter. If he spent the whole day carrying that one letter around, a hundred others would sit undelivered. Yet for a temporary reason, say nobody is home, a second visit does get the letter through. The two kinds of failure need two different treatments.

blocks.caption: One broken message keeps coming back and blocks the line

nodes.label: Queue
nodes.tip: All the messages wait in line here. The broken message comes back and takes the front again.

nodes.label: Worker
nodes.tip: Each time it tries the same job and hits the same exception.

nodes.label: SMS API
nodes.tip: The number itself is wrong, so this API will never respond no matter how often you try.

edges.label: The worker takes message #77
The SMS API says the number is wrong, 400
It failed, so the message goes straight back on the queue

blocks.body: Not all failures are equal: retry the temporary ones, set the permanent ones aside.

aside.title: The holiday-night SMS storm
aside.body: One app's SMS gateway was down for 10 minutes. The moment it came back, thousands of messages retried at once and knocked the gateway over again, because every retry was immediate and all of them fired at the same time.

items.meaning: A message that fails every time you run it, because the message itself is broken.
Many messages retrying together and pressing even harder on a service that is already down.

check.q: An SMS to a wrong number keeps failing. Why is retrying it forever a mistake?
check.a: The failure is permanent: the number won't fix itself, so a retry changes nothing. The message just keeps coming back and wasting the worker's and the API's time.

slides.title: Retry with backoff, and the DLQ at the end
slides.tldr: Retry a limited number of times, waiting twice as long each time. If it still fails, park the message in a dead-letter queue and let a human look.

blocks.title: The postman and the dead letter office
blocks.body: The postman goes back after a short wait, then after twice as long, then twice as long again. The gap grows each time, and some postmen go a little earlier or later so they don't all arrive at the same house at the same moment. If the letter still isn't delivered after three tries, it goes to the **dead letter office**, where a person looks at it and decides what to do.

blocks.caption: Messenger's default backoff: starts at 1s and doubles each time

items.label: 1st retry
items.tip: A temporary hiccup often clears up within a second.

items.label: 2nd retry
items.tip: The gap doubles, giving the failing service time to catch its breath.

items.label: 3rd retry
items.tip: If it still fails, the problem probably isn't temporary.

items.label: Failure transport
items.tip: max_retries is used up and the message is parked in a separate place. A human looks at it next.

blocks.body: Add up the waits: 1s + 2s + 4s is 7 seconds of patience. That rides out a blip, but not the 10-minute gateway outage from the story: every message would use up its retries and land in the DLQ. To ride out 10 minutes, start at 1 minute and keep doubling: waits of 1, 2, 4 and 8 minutes (`delay: 60000`, `max_retries: 4`) cover 15 minutes. The price is that a truly broken message now circles for 15 minutes before a human hears about it.

blocks.caption: The life of one message: from failure to resolution

steps.title: 1. Fails
steps.body: The handler throws, no ack is sent
steps.tip: Messenger understands the job wasn't done.

steps.title: 2. Waits
steps.body: The backoff delay grows and the message sits
steps.tip: This gives the failing service time to recover.

steps.title: 3. Retries
steps.body: Tries again, up to max_retries times
steps.tip: Without a limit, a broken message would circle forever.

steps.title: 4. DLQ
steps.body: The failed message is parked in its own queue
steps.tip: The main queue is clean again and keeps moving.

steps.title: 5. A human
steps.body: Fixes the cause, then replays or discards it
steps.tip: A message landing in the DLQ should always raise an alert.

aside.body: Grow the gap, cap the count, and move the stubborn message somewhere else.

items.meaning: Waiting longer before each retry than before the last one.
A small random plus or minus on the wait time so everyone doesn't arrive together.
Dead-letter queue: a separate home for messages that still fail after retries.

check.q: Why add jitter to a backoff?
check.a: If a thousand messages fail at the same moment, without jitter they all retry in the same second and knock the service over again. Jitter spreads them out.

slides.title: Retry strategy and failure transport in Messenger
slides.tldr: Set retry_strategy and failure_transport on the transport. Throw a plain exception for temporary failures and UnrecoverableMessageHandlingException for permanent ones.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        failure_transport: failed

        transports:
            async:
                dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
                retry_strategy:
                    max_retries: 3
                    delay: 1000        # first wait: 1 second
                    multiplier: 2      # 1s, 2s, 4s
                    max_delay: 60000   # never more than 1 minute
                    jitter: 0.1        # ±10% random
            failed: 'doctrine://default?queue_name=failed'

        routing:
            'App\Message\SendSms': async

marks.tip: Without this line, a message that uses up max_retries is simply thrown away and nobody even sees it.
No more retries than this number. After the last failure the message goes to the failure transport.
The home for failed messages. In a small app a Doctrine table is enough, and no extra worker is needed.
When it sees this exception, Messenger skips the retries and sends the message straight to the failure transport.
A normal exception or a transport exception triggers the retry strategy. Don't catch it here and swallow it.

items.desc: See the messages in the failure transport and why they failed
Send one specific message back to its original transport
Run all failed messages again, one by one
Delete a message you no longer need

items: Raise an alert when messages pile up in the failure transport. A DLQ that fills silently is lost work.
Fix the root cause before retrying, or the same message will fail and come back again.
A 4xx answer from an API, like the 400 in the story, is usually permanent: rethrow it as UnrecoverableMessageHandlingException. 5xx, timeouts and 429 are temporary.
The config above shows Messenger's defaults, 7 seconds of retrying in all. Choose `delay` and `max_retries` from the longest outage you want to survive.

check.q: Which exception should you throw for a message with an invalid phone number, and what does it do?
check.a: `UnrecoverableMessageHandlingException`. Messenger skips the retries and sends the message straight to the failure transport, because retrying can't fix the number.

slides.title: The trap: work done twice after a retry
slides.tldr: Retries and redeliveries mean a handler can run more than once. Record the message id in a processed-message table so the work happens only once.

blocks.title: The corner shop's delivery ledger
blocks.body: The shopkeeper writes a number on every delivery slip. When someone shows up twice with slip 102, he opens the ledger, sees "102 was already collected", and doesn't hand over the goods a second time. For an **idempotent consumer**, that ledger is the `processed_message` table.

marks.tip: Every run adds points. A user on 100 points who should get +50 ends on 200, not 150, when the message arrives twice.
With `PRIMARY KEY (message_id, handler)` on the table, one message gets into one handler only once.
0 rows inserted means it was already done, so quietly return. This is not a failure.
The work and the ledger entry are in one transaction, so one can't happen without the other.

blocks.body: Where there are retries there are duplicates, and handling duplicates is the handler's job.

items: External work like email or a payment API can't join your DB transaction. Give the provider an idempotency key there.
The producer creates the message id (`Uuid::v7()`). The id must stay the same across retries; make a new one and the check is useless.
The table only grows. Delete rows older than the longest a message can still be redelivered, or it becomes a storage bill.

use: Handlers that add, charge, send or create something, where running twice does harm.
avoid: Handlers that set a value, like "status = paid". They are already safe to repeat, and the table adds a write per message.

check.q: Why is the UNIQUE constraint on (message_id, handler) in processed_message, not on message_id alone?
check.a: One message can go to several handlers. With a unique message_id alone, the first handler would mark it and the other handlers could never do their work.

slides.title: The 2 a.m. report and a server restart halfway
slides.tldr: Run one huge job in a single go and a mid-run crash means starting over. Run cron on two servers and the job runs twice.

blocks.title: The giant wedding pot
blocks.body: For a wedding, food for 1000 guests goes into one enormous pot. If the stove dies halfway, the whole pot is thrown out and the cooking starts again. A smart cook uses 20 small pots and ticks each one off in a notebook when it's done. If the stove dies, only the pot on the fire goes back on.

blocks.caption: When a one-shot job crashes, it starts over from scratch every time

actors.label: Cron
actors.tip: The clock that starts the job at a set time.

actors.label: Report job
actors.tip: Processes every user's data in a single go.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Where the 1 million rows are being read from.

messages.label: 02:00 start the report
messages.tip: The call that comes at the same time every night.

blocks.body: Break big work into small pieces, and write down where you are after every piece.

aside.title: Two servers, two payroll emails
aside.body: A company had a cron job that emailed payslips at the end of each month. After the app was moved onto two servers, the same cron ran on both, and everyone received two emails.

items.meaning: Work done by a worker outside the web request.
A saved mark showing how far the work has got.

check.q: What is the main weakness of a job that processes 1 million rows in one go?
check.a: If it stops midway, it loses all its progress and must start over each time. With small pieces and a checkpoint, only the piece in progress runs again.

slides.title: Visibility timeout and priority
slides.tldr: When a worker takes a message it is hidden for a while, and if no ack arrives in time another worker gets it. Urgent work in its own queue never waits behind slow work.

blocks.title: The cook takes a pot
blocks.body: Once a cook picks up a pot, nobody else touches it, because it's his now. But if he doesn't bring it back within the agreed time, the manager assumes he has gone missing and gives the pot to someone else. That agreed time is the **visibility timeout**. The manager also keeps a separate "urgent pot" shelf, so a guest's coffee doesn't get stuck behind the pasta.

blocks.caption: Visibility timeout: if a worker dies, the message goes to someone else

actors.label: Queue
actors.tip: Stores messages and remembers who has been holding each one, and for how long.

actors.label: Worker A
actors.tip: Takes the message first, then dies midway.

actors.label: Worker B
actors.tip: Gets the same message once the time is up.

messages.label: Message #9, hidden for 30s
messages.tip: For these 30 seconds nobody else can see the message.

blocks.title: Two rules
items: Set the timeout longer than the longest the job can take. Too short, and the message passes to someone else while the job is still running, so you get duplicates.
Keep urgent and slow work in separate queues, and have the worker read the urgent queue first.
On SQS the transport option is `visibility_timeout`; on the Doctrine transport it is `redeliver_timeout`.
Splitting long jobs into pieces lets you keep the timeout short.
The job takes 5 minutes but the timeout is 30 seconds: someone else picks up the message while the job is still running.
A timeout that is far too long has a price too: after a worker dies, the message waits out the whole timeout before anyone retries it.

check.q: A job takes up to 2 minutes, and the visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What happens?
check.a: The worker is still working, but after 30 seconds the message becomes visible again and another worker gets it. The same job then runs in two places.

slides.title: Symfony Scheduler and priority transports
slides.tldr: Instead of cron, keep the schedule in code, use a lock so it runs on only one server, and give urgent work its own transport.

blocks.body: Without a lock, two servers that each run a Scheduler worker both release `BuildDailyReport` at 02:00: two reports and two payslip emails. With a lock, the first worker takes it and the second finds it taken and skips. The price: the lock only works if `framework.lock` points at a store all servers share, such as Redis or the database. The default local store protects nothing across servers. The simplest alternative is to run just one Scheduler worker under a supervisor, at the cost that nothing is released while it is down.

marks.tip: 2 a.m. Phoenix time. Without a time zone, the server's time is used.
`stateful` remembers the last run time, so runs missed while the worker was down come back.
Thanks to the lock, even with workers on several servers the job is released only once per slot.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        transports:
            high: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%?queue_name=high'
            low:  '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%?queue_name=low'
        routing:
            'App\Message\SendOtp': high        # the user is waiting
            'App\Message\BuildDailyReport': low # fine if it's late

# worker: high first, then low when high is empty
#   php bin/console messenger:consume high low
#   php bin/console messenger:consume scheduler_default

marks.tip: Work like an OTP goes on the high queue, so it never gets stuck behind hundreds of thousands of reports.
The order of the transport names is the priority: high is always emptied first.

items.desc: See every schedule and its next run time
The worker that releases the scheduled messages

items: `RecurringMessage::cron()` needs the `dragonmantank/cron-expression` package.
A Scheduler job is just a Messenger message, so retries and the failure transport apply to it too.
Test the lock by starting two `scheduler_default` workers on different machines. If the job is released twice, the lock store is not shared.

check.q: With workers on two servers, how do you stop a Scheduler job from being released twice?
check.a: Add `->lock(...)` to the schedule so only one worker can release the message at a time. Add `stateful()` as well and you don't need to worry about missed runs either.

slides.title: The trap: one giant job in a single go
slides.tldr: Split big work into small chunks. Each chunk is one message, and the next chunk's message carries a checkpoint (the last id), so a crash reruns only the current chunk.

blocks.body: The 2 a.m. report has 1 million rows (ids 1 to 1,000,000). In chunks of 500 that is 2,000 small messages. If the server dies after 600,000 rows, the broker hands out chunk 1,201 again, which carries `afterId` 600000, and only 500 rows are redone instead of 600,000. The price: 2,000 trips through the queue instead of one loop, and chunks run one after another, so the total is a little slower. A 10-second job doesn't need this.

marks.tip: Memory runs out, the visibility timeout passes, and a crash means 1 million rows again.
Start after the last id, not with OFFSET. The query is just as fast at the millionth row.
A rerun of a chunk must give the same result, because redelivery can happen.
The checkpoint goes into the next chunk's message. If the job crashes, it starts again from here.

blocks.body: Keep chunks small, keep chunks idempotent, and write down your progress.

items: Size chunks so each one finishes in a few seconds; that keeps both memory and the timeout safe.
You can also fan out the next chunks with a Messenger batch handler instead of dispatching them yourself, but this cursor style is simple and safe.
`LIMIT 500 OFFSET n` gets slow at a large n, and if new rows arrive in between, rows get skipped or duplicated.

check.q: Which two properties let a chunked job safely rerun after a crash?
check.a: Each chunk is idempotent, so running twice gives the same result. And the next message carries a checkpoint, so it continues from the last position instead of redoing everything.

slides.title: Seeing your jobs: what to measure
slides.tldr: Background jobs die quietly. Measure queue depth, the age of the oldest message, the failure rate and the run time, and set alerts on them.

blocks.body: A queue holding 10 messages is nothing, and 100,000 that grows by 500 a minute is a flood. But 10 messages can still hurt if the oldest has waited 30 minutes. So alert on how long work waits, not only on how many items there are.

blocks.caption: Four signals for background jobs

rows.tip: A growing backlog means the workers can't keep up with the flow, or every worker has died.

cells: How far behind the work is
rows.tip: This is the delay the user actually feels. The age can be high even when the depth is small.
It is the first thing to jump after a bad deploy or when an external API breaks.
Even one message here means a piece of work was quietly dropped.

marks.tip: Messenger fires this event whenever a worker fails on a message.
If `will_retry` is false, the message is heading to the DLQ, which deserves its own alert.

blocks.file: age of the oldest message (Doctrine transport, PostgreSQL)

marks.tip: Rows are deleted on ack, so the oldest row is the longest-waiting or longest-stuck message. Alert when this passes your limit, say 5 minutes for emails.

items.desc: How many messages are waiting in each transport
See the failed messages and their causes

items: On SQS the same number is the CloudWatch metric `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage`.

aside.body: Not the queue depth but the age of the oldest message tells you how far behind the user is.

check.q: Only 10 messages are waiting in the queue, yet the app has a problem. Which measure would tell you why?
check.a: The age of the oldest message. If even one of those 10 has been sitting for half an hour, a worker is stuck, even though the depth looks fine.

slides.title: Two more servers, and old code keeps running
slides.tldr: Extra workers on extra servers share one queue for free. But the deploy that restarts them signals through a local cache, so only one server hears it.

blocks.title: One ticket rail, three kitchens
blocks.body: A pizza place hangs every order ticket on one rail. Ryan opens a second and a third kitchen, and the cooks in all three take the next ticket from that same rail. Each ticket goes to exactly one cook, so three kitchens serve three times the orders with no new planning. The surprise: every kitchen has its own notice board, and the manager pinned "new recipe from today" on the first kitchen's board only.

blocks.caption: After a deploy with a local cache, server 2 keeps running version 1

blocks.title: Four more surprises on the way
items: A handler saves a file on server 1, the next job runs on server 2, and the file is not there.
A worker lives for hours, not for one request, so a small memory leak or a stale in-memory value adds up.
Every worker holds a database connection, so more servers means more connections to one database.
All workers read one transport, so at some point the queue itself, not the workers, is the limit.

aside.title: The field that nobody read
aside.body: A team added a field to a message and deployed. Server 1 restarted its workers and handled it. Server 2 kept the old handler, which ignored the field, and nobody noticed for three days.

items.meaning: Many workers read one queue, and each message goes to just one of them.
A long-running PHP process started by `messenger:consume`.

check.q: After a deploy, server 1 runs the new code but server 2 does not. What went wrong with the stop signal?
check.a: `messenger:stop-workers` writes its mark into the cache of the server it runs on. With a filesystem cache that is server 1's disk, so workers on server 2 never see it.

slides.title: One shared place for the stop signal
slides.tldr: The stop command leaves a mark in the app cache and workers read it. Put the cache where every server can see it, or restart per server, or replace containers.

blocks.body: `messenger:stop-workers` never talks to a worker. It writes a timestamp into the app cache (`cache.app`). Every worker looks there between messages, and when the mark is newer than its own start, it finishes the message it is on and exits. A supervisor then starts a fresh process on the new code. So the signal reaches exactly the workers that read the same cache.

blocks.caption: One command, one shared cache, every worker on every server

nodes.label: Deploy script
nodes.tip: Runs the stop command once per release.

nodes.label: Shared cache
nodes.tip: The one place the restart mark is written and read. Every server can reach it.

nodes.label: Worker, server 1
nodes.tip: Checks the cache between messages.

nodes.label: Worker, server 2
nodes.tip: On another machine, reading the same cache.

nodes.label: Worker, server 3
nodes.tip: Also on its own machine, also reading the same cache.

edges.label: The deploy runs stop-workers, which writes a restart mark into the shared cache.
Worker 1 sees the mark after its current message and exits.
Worker 2, on another server, sees the same mark and exits.
Worker 3 does too. The supervisor then starts all of them on the new code.

blocks.code:
framework:
    cache:
        # cache.app also carries the stop signal. Its default is a folder
        # on THIS server's disk, so other servers never see the mark.
        app: cache.adapter.redis
        default_redis_provider: '%env(REDIS_URL)%'

marks.tip: Redis is reachable from every server, so one stop-workers call is seen by all of them.

blocks.title: Three ways to refresh workers on a deploy
items: **Shared cache:** run `php bin/console messenger:stop-workers` once. Price: every server needs that cache, and while it is down the signal does not arrive.
**Per server:** the deploy runs the stop command, or `supervisorctl restart`, on every server. Price: the script must know every server, and a skipped one stays stale.
**Replace containers:** a rolling deploy starts new containers and stops the old ones. Price: you need an orchestrator, and old containers need time to finish their job.

blocks.body: A stop signal sent through a cache reaches only the workers that read that same cache.

items.desc: Ask all workers on the same cache to exit after their current message
Restart this server's workers, one by one, gracefully

items: Workers finish the message they are on, so a deploy does not cut a job in half.
The command only makes workers exit. Without a supervisor, nobody starts them again.

check.q: You run `messenger:stop-workers` once, with workers on three servers. What must hold for all of them to restart?
check.a: All three must read the same cache, and each server needs a supervisor that starts a new process once the old one exits.

slides.title: Keeping workers alive, and how many to run
slides.tldr: Work out the worker count from jobs per second and job time, then let a supervisor run that many and restart them. The flags make each worker retire cleanly.

blocks.body: Say the team must handle **40 jobs a second**, and a job takes **0.5 s**. One worker finishes 2 jobs a second, so 40 ÷ 2 = **20 workers busy at all times**. With only 10, 20 jobs a second get done and 20 wait: the queue grows by 1,200 a minute. Add about 30% headroom (26) and round up to 27: 3 servers × 9 workers. The price is 27 database connections and up to 9 × 128 MB = about 1.1 GB of memory per server.

blocks.code:
; same file on all 3 servers: 3 x 9 = 27 workers
[program:messenger-async]
directory=/var/www/app
command=php bin/console messenger:consume async --time-limit=900 --memory-limit=128M --limit=500
process_name=%(program_name)s_%(process_num)02d
numprocs=9
user=www-data
environment=APP_ENV="prod"
autostart=true
autorestart=true
startsecs=0
startretries=10
stopsignal=TERM
stopwaitsecs=60

marks.tip: Each flag makes a worker exit on purpose: after 15 minutes, past 128 MB (checked between messages), or after 500 messages. A leak cannot grow for days.
Nine copies on this server. The same file on three servers gives 27.
Whenever a worker exits, for any reason, the supervisor starts a new one.
After TERM, the supervisor waits up to 60 s for the current job. Keep it above your slowest job.

blocks.body: Let every worker retire on schedule, and let a supervisor hire the next one.

items: `--time-limit` is also a safety net: even if a stop signal is lost, workers run new code within 15 minutes.
With systemd, use a template unit with `Restart=always`, and the same flags.
Graceful stop on TERM needs the `pcntl` PHP extension.

items.meaning: A small program that starts your workers and starts them again when they exit.

check.q: You need 30 jobs a second and each job takes 0.2 s. How many workers must be busy, and what happens with 4?
check.a: 30 × 0.2 = 6 workers busy at all times. Four workers finish only 20 jobs a second, so the queue grows by 10 a second, 600 a minute.

slides.title: The trap: state that lives on one server
slides.tldr: A file on one server's disk or a value cached in a worker's memory breaks on many servers. Send IDs, keep files in shared storage, cache with a TTL.

blocks.body: On one server, the job that builds an invoice PDF and the job that emails it always ran side by side, so a path on local disk worked. On three servers, the queue hands the second job to any worker, and the file sits on only one of them. Also, a worker lives for hours, so a value kept in a property stays until the process ends. The fix: the message carries the invoice **ID**, the file goes to storage every server can reach, and cached values get a TTL. The price: a network call instead of a local read, and one more dependency.

marks.tip: A property lives as long as the worker. The rate read at 9 a.m. is still used at 9 p.m.
This writes to the local disk of whichever server runs the job.
A path means nothing on another server.
Shared storage: every server reads and writes the same files. Price: a network call, and one more thing that can fail.
The cache pool has a TTL, so a value is at most 5 minutes old, even in a worker that lives for hours.
The message carries only the ID. The email handler fetches the file from storage.

blocks.body: Messages carry IDs. Files live in shared storage. A job never needs one server's disk.

items: Symfony resets services tagged `kernel.reset` after each message, but your own properties are not reset.
If a value must be fresh, read it through a cache pool with a TTL instead of a property.
Writing to `var/` or `/tmp` in one handler and reading it in another message.
A memory leak: that is what `--memory-limit` and `--limit` from the last slide catch.

check.q: Why is `new EmailInvoice($path)` with a local path a bug once there are three servers?
check.a: The next job may run on another server, where that path does not exist. Send the ID and fetch the file from storage that all servers share.

slides.title: When the transport or the database is the limit
slides.tldr: Watch queue depth and message age to know when to add workers. Each worker costs a database connection, and the transport must keep up, so choose it by volume.

blocks.body: Watch two numbers: queue depth (`php bin/console messenger:stats`, if the transport can count) and the age of the oldest message. Depth rising while every worker is busy means add workers. But each worker holds about one database connection. 3 servers × 9 workers is 27, and PostgreSQL allows 100 by default. If the web app peaks at 40, that leaves 60, so about 6 servers of 9. Past that, run fewer workers or put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front, at the price of one more thing to run. The transport has limits too:

High volume, no server to run

Failed messages and retries are a separate topic, covered in the retries lesson.

check.q: You run the Doctrine transport with 40 workers on 5 servers, and the web app gets slow. What did the workers add?
check.a: Each holds a database connection and polls the messages table about once a second, so your main database carries that load. Cut workers, or move to Redis, RabbitMQ or SQS.

slides.title: Five SMS for one order, and the one that mattered never arrived
slides.tldr: Blast every event to every channel and users get fed up and opt out. Then when a provider breaks, the urgent message is the one that gets lost.

blocks.title: The neighborhood pharmacy's news
blocks.body: For one medicine order, the pharmacy phones and texts the same customer at every step: order received, packed, on the way, arrived. In the end the customer blocks his number. Then the day some urgent insulin actually arrives, the call doesn't connect and nobody tries another way. A notification system's job is to tell the right person, through the right channel, once.

blocks.caption: News of the same order: everyone on every channel vs organized

columns.title: What many people do
items: Placed, paid, packed, shipped, delivered: 5 SMS and 5 emails
The user turned SMS off, and it still goes out
A retry sends the same message twice
When the SMS provider is down, the OTP never arrives
columns.tip: Fire on every channel whenever something happens. Easy to build, but tiring for the user.

columns.title: What should happen
items: Urgent events stand alone, the rest go into one digest
It goes only through the channel the user picked
A dedup key means the same message goes once
If a provider breaks, the message isn't dropped but takes a fallback
columns.tip: Each message follows the user's preferences, goes out once, and takes a fallback route when something breaks.

blocks.body: A notification's job isn't to send messages. It is to tell the right person, through the right channel, exactly once.

items.meaning: A one-time code, usually sent by SMS, that proves it is really you, such as a login or password-reset code.
The user's choice to stop receiving some kind of message.

aside.title: The digital wallet's annoyance
aside.body: A payment app sent a push, an SMS and an email for every small transaction. Within a few months many users switched off all messages, and then nobody received the urgent security alerts either.
Something happening and telling the user about it are two separate decisions. The second has to weigh preferences, repetition, load and provider failures.

check.q: When users get fed up with too many notifications, what is the biggest loss?
check.a: They switch off all messages, so later the urgent ones (OTP, security) no longer reach them either.

blocks.body: The pharmacy notebook says: Ryan wants to be told by phone only, and never after 9 p.m. Before telling anyone, the pharmacist checks the notebook, checks whether the same news went out yesterday, and only then calls. If the call doesn't connect, he tries the emergency contact's number. Every step is a separate decision.

`Recipient` holds both the email and the phone; each channel uses the one it needs.

framework:
    notifier:
        texter_transports:
            # if the first fails, the second; if both fail, an exception
            sms: 'failover(%env(SMS_PROVIDER_A_DSN)% %env(SMS_PROVIDER_B_DSN)%)'
        channel_policy:
            urgent: ['sms', 'email']
            high: ['email']
            low: ['email']

marks.tip: `failover(...)` tries them in order. No code changes, only the DSN.
If you give no channels, the Notification's importance picks the channels according to this policy.

items.meaning: One line that says which provider to use and how to log in to it, like a connection string.

items: Each SMS provider has its own DSN. If Notifier has no bridge for yours, you can write a small transport yourself.
Mailer has a `failover(...)` DSN too, with the same idea.
Notifier sends synchronously. Route it through Messenger so the request doesn't slow down.
Failover can send twice if provider A delivered but answered too late. For an OTP that is harmless; keep it in mind for anything else.

items.label: When sending fails: retries and the DLQ

check.q: Do you have to change code to add a second SMS provider in Notifier?
check.a: No. Just turn the `texter_transports` DSN into `failover(A B)`. If the first provider fails, Notifier automatically tries the second.

slides.title: The OTP must get through: transactional vs marketing
slides.tldr: If every message obeys preferences, a user who switched notifications off never gets the login code. Mark messages transactional or not, and let only transactional ones skip preferences.

blocks.body: Rachel switched off every notification because the offers annoyed her. Now she asks for a password-reset code, and a pipeline that obeys her preferences quietly sends nothing. She is locked out and no error appears anywhere. The fix is to decide per message **kind**: a transactional message (one the user needs to finish what they came to do) skips preferences, and everything else obeys them.

marks.tip: Right for a promotion, wrong for an OTP: the user asked for this code a moment ago.
The list is explicit and short on purpose. Adding a kind here is a decision someone should review.
Transactional kinds ignore preferences. Everything else still asks the user.

blocks.title: What it costs
items: Keep the transactional list short. Once a promotion sneaks in, you are ignoring opt-outs, which can break the law.
Give OTPs their own limit (say 5 an hour per number), or an attacker can make you pay for thousands of SMS.
They skip the digest too: a code inside an hourly summary is useless.

aside.body: Marketing asks permission. An OTP answers a request.

check.q: Why may a password-reset OTP ignore opt-out while a promotion may not?
check.a: The user asked for the OTP a moment ago and cannot go on without it. A promotion is something we want to say, so the user decides whether to hear it.

slides.title: The same message once, and a digest when there are too many
slides.tldr: Retries and redeliveries send a message twice, so stop that with a dedup key. Past the limit, ordinary messages are held back by a rate limiter and collected in a digest.

blocks.body: Sending a notification is message processing too, so a retry can send the same SMS twice. The fix is a **dedup key** (for example `order_shipped:501:user7`) that goes into a UNIQUE table only once. And once a user would receive more than three in an hour, the rest of the ordinary messages aren't sent immediately but collected in a digest. Urgent ones skip that limit.

marks.tip: With UNIQUE on dedup_key, the second message can't get in.
Past the limit an ordinary message goes to the digest; an urgent one (an OTP) skips the limit. Nothing is lost; it just goes out later.
If sending fails, we remove the mark. Otherwise the retry is skipped and the message is never sent.

blocks.code:
framework:
    rate_limiter:
        per_user:
            policy: 'sliding_window'
            limit: 3
            interval: '1 hour'

marks.tip: At most 3 notifications per person per hour. The autowire name is `$perUserLimiter`.

items: Set the dedup mark before sending and forget to remove it when sending fails, and the message is lost for good.
What the digest collects must be sent on time: the next slide shows the scheduled job that empties it.

items.meaning: Counts how often something happens in a time window and says no once the limit is passed.

check.q: Which is right for building a dedup key: a random UUID or the identity of the event?
check.a: The identity of the event, such as `order_shipped:501:user7`. A retry produces the same key, which is how the duplicate is caught; a random UUID is new each time and makes the check useless.

slides.title: Emptying the digest: a scheduled job
slides.tldr: A digest helps only if something sends it. A Scheduler task gathers each user's waiting items every hour, sends one message, and clears them only after the send worked.

blocks.body: Messages held back by the limit sit in the digest table. Left alone they never reach anyone, which is the same as dropping them. A scheduled task runs every hour and sends each user one summary. It clears the items only after the send worked, so a failure just means the digest goes out in the next run.

marks.tip: Symfony Scheduler runs this class every hour. It needs a running worker, or nothing ever fires.
If the send throws, this line never runs and the items wait for the next hour. Clearing first would lose them.

blocks.title: What it costs
items: The digest arrives up to an hour late. Fine for updates, wrong for anything urgent.
A crash between the send and the clear sends the same digest twice. For a summary email that is acceptable.
Without a running Scheduler worker, the digest silently never leaves.

items.desc: start the worker that fires scheduled tasks

check.q: Why does the job clear the digest items only after the send succeeded?
check.a: If it cleared first and the send then failed, the items would be gone and the user would never hear about them. Clearing last means a failure just retries next hour.
